question: What is the meaning of composition in relation to technical data and reports?
description: The composition refers to the percentage of raw material that an object consists of. This information is crucial for understanding the material makeup of a product or component. It is typically expressed as a decimal or integer value, indicating the proportion of each raw material used in the object's construction. This data is essential for various purposes, including material tracking, environmental impact assessments, and compliance with regulations. It can be found in manufacturer information or Environmental Product Declarations, which provide detailed insights into the materials used in products.

information in order to balance costs against value. A social 
cost-benefit analysis can support this by determining the desirable 
overhead (Bouwend Nederland, 2020).  
• Standardized exchange: There is a lack of standardization in passports 
that support the linkage and exchange of data among different 
passport stakeholders across supply chains (Anastasiades et al., 
2021; Chahine, 2021; Charef and Emmitt, 2020; Damen, 2012; 
Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Gonçalves et al., 2021; Heisel and 
Rau-Oberhuber, 2020; Holla, 2021; Kedir et al., 2021; Kovacic et al., 
2019; Lützkendorf, 2019; Munaro and Tavares, 2021; Pibal et al., 
2021; Sesana et al., 2020; Wandiga, 2020). This is caused by pass­
ports using their individual data formats, passport taxonomies and 
guidelines (Dourlens-Quaranta et al., 2020; Holla, 2021; Kedir et al., 
2021), dot have linking identifiers (Anastasiades et al., 2021), reg­
ister in different nomenclature (e.g., component terminology, ma­
terial taxonomy) and have a different unit of analysis (e.g., which 
parts together form a building, component, element or material 
(Honic et al., 2019b)) (Debacker and Manshoven, 2016; Ganter and 
Lützkendorf, 2019; Honic et al., 2019a; Kedir et al., 2021; Kovacic 
et al., 2020; Munaro et al., 2019), functional unit, scope definitions 
and system boundaries (Honic et al., 2019d; Kovacic et al., 2019). 
Different viewpoints exist toward the limited standardization prob­
lem. Some papers propose to create passport ontologies (Ashino, 
2010; Kedir et al., 2021; Munaro and Tavares, 2021). Most others 
argue that standardization is too difficult because of regional dif­
ferences, stakeholder requirements, social characteristics, economic 
environment, and geo-political reasons (Bouwend Nederland, 2020; 
Timmermans and Epstein, 2010). For example, the goal, the scope, 
the stakeholders and which degree of material reuse is pursued 
(Bouwend Nederland, 2020), the life cycle phase (Wittenveen & Bos, 
2018), the recovery option (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018), and the type of 
materials or components that are used in an object (concrete has 
specifications that require less specific data than a condensing boiler 
(Wittenveen & Bos, 2018)) can differ. Transferability is also a key 
design consideration (Gonçalves et al., 2021) as data needs to remain 
available after systems change, merge, or discontinue (Munaro and 
Tavares, 2021).
